title: 18 months into building a fantasy-sports-meets-idle-RPG, here's the four-tool AI stack I've landed on. Curious where others have landed
author: iiithewizardiii
selftext:
https://preview.redd.it/0k4ffuw75k1h1.png?width=1101&format=png&auto=webp&s=024fbf502440a8430a5a257ea00e5bafcd960060

I'm a solo dev working on **Fantasy Fantasy** — a web-based persistent multiplayer game that crosses fantasy sports (draft a roster, set a lineup, play a season) with idle RPG progression (a world that runs while you're not logged in). Eleven Houses, one league, one world. Pre-launch, in the public-building phase.

The only reason this project exists at solo scale is that I stopped trying to make one model do everything and started picking a different AI tool for each layer of the game, letting each one do what it's actually good at. 18 months in, I have strong opinions about which tool wins where, when each one hits a wall, and where I still have to drive manually.

# The stack at a glance

|Layer|Primary tool|Why this one|
|:-|:-|:-|
|**Code**|Claude (Sonnet, with occasional Opus passes)|Best long-context reasoning over my actual codebase. Refuses to hallucinate APIs I haven't installed.|
|**Art**|Midjourney for stills, Grok Imagine + a couple of others for animations|MJ's `--sref` consistency is the only reason my 11 Houses look like 11 Houses and not 11 random LoRAs|
|**Game balance**|Perplexity as the orchestrator, with Claude and ChatGPT underneath as the actual reasoners|I let the orchestrator pick which model answers based on the question. Cheaper and the answers are better than either model alone.|
|**Lore expansion**|Perplexity, again — but a totally different workflow|Worldbuilding is iterative. I wrote the canon. The model expands within it.|

I'll walk through each one.

  
1. Code — Claude

I write everything in **Replit** with **Claude** as the pair. Stack is TypeScript end-to-end — React/Vite on the front, Node/Express + Drizzle/Postgres on the back — and version control runs through Replit's checkpoint and task-merge flow rather than a manual GitHub workflow.

**What works:**

* Claude is the only model I trust to read my actual repo before answering. When I paste in three or four files of context and ask "where's the bug," it doesn't invent a function that doesn't exist. ChatGPT and Gemini both still do this for me regularly (or used to-- I haven't tried 5.5 yet).
* Long-running refactors. I can hand Claude a 600-line file and ask it to extract a feature into its own module, and it'll come back with a diff that *applies*. The first time that happened cleanly I sat there for thirty seconds in a state of mild shock.
* The "explain why you did that" follow-up. Most other models tell you what they did. Claude tells you what it considered and didn't do-- but it didn't start doing that until late last year.

**Where it hits a wall:**

* Game state machines. Anything with more than three or four concurrent state branches starts to lose threads. I've had to start tasks asynchronously and make them wait before proceeding as tasks worked with different states.
* Anything with timing-sensitive math (idle accrual, tick rates, offline catch-up). I write the prompts with the basic math myself, Claude writes the implementation, I write the tests, we iterate.

**Cost reality:** Code is by far my biggest AI spend. Roughly 70% of my total monthly AI bill goes here.

Anyone running a different code model as their daily driver and finding it equally good on long-context refactors? I keep meaning to give Cursor + a different backend a real two-week trial and I keep not doing it because the current setup works. Has always nagged at me.

# 2. Art — Midjourney for stills, a stack of tools for motion

Eleven Houses, each with a palette, a sigil, a motto, and a signature character. 200 named characters in the canon, every one with a completed portrait. All of them generated in Midjourney, all of them carrying the same locked style. That's the part most people don't believe until they scroll the roster.

https://preview.redd.it/qqoacene5k1h1.png?width=2360&format=png&auto=webp&s=bd5cc45cb426f9decc577be81e41d6e52c9fefb8

**Why MJ over the alternatives:**

* `--sref` (style reference). I have one master sref code that defines the "polished fantasy" aesthetic of the game. Every portrait carries it. That's the only reason my 11 Houses don't look like 11 different artists worked on them.
* Moodboards. Continuing to put the best of the outputs into a MJ Moodboard that is coupled with the sref locks in the look.
* Painterly hero portraits without prompt acrobatics. SDXL gets close but I'm spending more time prompt-engineering and less time drawing characters.
* `--ar` flexibility for the actual UI shapes I need (4:5 portraits, 1:1 banners, 16:9 spreads).

**My MJ pipeline (the actual workflow, not the marketing version):**

1. Write the prompt in a structured template (House, role, stats, distinctive feature, color palette, sref code, ar, stylize value)
2. Generate 4 variants
3. If none land, adjust stylize or chaos and reroll — never the prompt
4. If the prompt itself was wrong, I rewrite it with a Perplexity-assisted critique pass — I literally paste the prompt + the image into Perplexity and ask "why didn't this land the brief"
5. Upscale, then dump to Google Drive via a [Make.com](http://Make.com) automation
6. Photoshop pass for the things AI still can't do — fixing eyes that drift, finger counts, the occasional background crazytown inclusions

**Motion / animation:**  
For character motion I'm using **Grok Imagine** (image-to-video, then extend-from-frame chaining for longer shots). For UI motion / interface animations I'm doing it the old-fashioned way in code with CSS and Framer.

The honest truth on animation: it's the weakest part of my pipeline. Grok Imagine is the best of the current options for what I'm doing but it's still 6/10. Faces drift. Hands re-render. I'm shipping the launch trailer with maybe 60% of the animations I originally wanted because the other 40% weren't worth the credits to fix.

**Hard-earned lesson:** Pick ONE consistency anchor (in my case `--sref + MJ Moodboard`) and don't deviate. Every time I've tried to use a "better" model for one character to save time, I've ended up with a character that doesn't belong to the family.

What's everyone using for character animation right now? I keep hearing about Kling, Runway, Pika, Sora, Veo — I've tried most of them at the trial level and none of them have been good enough to displace Grok Imagine for my use case (specifically character motion at portrait crop, painterly aesthetic-- I'm not making an action game or this part of my stack would be way different). If you've cracked that nut, I'd like to hear what your workflow is.

# 3. Game balance — Perplexity orchestrating Claude + ChatGPT underneath

This is the most underrated part of my stack and I think it's the one that might be most helpful.

**The problem:** Balancing a game with 8 stats, 6 starting positions + 1 Option slot + 2 Bench, 11 Houses, and a Stronghold tower-defense layer is a multi-dimensional math problem. I can't hold the whole state in my head and I can't trust one model to do it either, because each model has different weaknesses.

**What I do:**

I run balance questions through **Perplexity** as my orchestrator. Perplexity has a feature where you can ask a question and it'll route it through Claude or ChatGPT (and others) depending on the question type, and bring in live data if the question touches on existing F2P games. So for a question like *"if I cap Strength contribution at 60% of damage rolls, what happens to my caster builds over a 30-round arc"*, I get back:

* The math reasoning (Claude does this best — it'll actually keep the constraints straight)
* The market context (sourced — "in Idle Heroes, the equivalent cap was set at X% and here's what happened to caster usage rates")
* The dissenting view (often ChatGPT, which is more aggressive about pointing out edge cases Claude misses)

Then I take that synthesis and run it back through Claude *separately* with my actual balance spreadsheet attached, and ask it to recalculate.

**Cost vs. benefit:** This costs more per question than just asking Claude. But the answers are dramatically better, and "dramatically better" in a balance question means I don't have to re-balance the same system three weeks later. The math compounds.

**Where it breaks:** Anything that requires actual playtesting. No model on earth can tell you whether your roster meta is fun. You have to play it. AI assists balance; it doesn't replace playtest.

Is anyone else running an orchestrator-on-top-of-model-zoo workflow for balance? I feel like this is the most undertalked-about pattern in solo gamedev right now and I can't tell if that's because nobody's doing it or because everyone's quietly doing it and not posting about it.

# 4. Lore — Perplexity, different workflow

This is the layer where the AI/human split is evolving faster than i can keep track of.

**What I write:** The canon. The 11 House mottos, the sigils, the major characters' arcs, the cosmology (the Veils, the Black Halls, the Fallen registry), the truth statements ("Thornveil keeps score"), the tagline ("Your Fantasy League. In a Fantasy World.").

I write it. I rewrite it. I delete it. I bring it back. No model touches the canon (or the deep canon? Not sure what to call it).

**What Perplexity does:** Expansion within constraints.

Once a House has a motto and a palette, I'll ask Perplexity something like *"Given House Resolve's motto 'Stand, bleed, never break' and Tank-heavy combat identity, give me three new minor characters who feel earned by the House but aren't reskins of each other."* Perplexity comes back with named characters, brief backstories, and stat suggestions. I keep maybe one in five. The other four get scrapped or merged.

**Why Perplexity over the chat models for this:**

* It cites. Even fictional citations sometimes pull from real-world cultural reference points that strengthen the worldbuilding (a House motto that echoes a real historical oath reads richer than one that doesn't).
* It's more willing to say "this conflicts with what you established earlier" when I've fed it the canon docs. The chat models tend to " yes and" you and while that's good sometimes, it doesn't always work.

**Hard lesson:** I tried to AI-generate the canon early on. It was forgettable. Generic fantasy slop. You can tell within two sentences whether a piece of worldbuilding was written by a human who cared or generated by a model that didn't. I rewrote the entire foundational lore by hand around month 6 and the game changed. And I have to evolve it as we go, which tends to involve both me writing and models expanding. 

*Open question for the sub:* Curious where everyone else has landed the human/AI line on narrative. I draw it at canon (mine) vs. expansion (AI within mine). Has anyone gone further in either direction — fully human, or fully AI — and been happy with it?

# What I'd do differently if I started today

1. **Pick consistency anchor first, before generating one image.** The `--sref` lock saved me thousands of credits and weeks of rework. If you don't have one, your art will not look like a game — it'll look like a Pinterest board.
2. **Don't let AI write your canon.** Let it expand on it and inside it.
3. **Use an orchestrator, not a single model.** Picking the right model per question type is a \~30% quality jump for \~10% more cost.
4. **Build the test harness before the feature.** AI writes implementations faster than I can write tests. The bottleneck is now QA, not code. If I'd known that in year one, I'd have built better test infrastructure. But to be fair, the quality improvements in the last 12 months have made building better test infra way easier. 
5. **Don't apologize for the AI parts in your marketing.** Most players don't care that you used AI (regardless of the loud AI haters that invariably end up in your comments). They care if the game is good. The people who care that you used AI are other devs — which is why I'm saying this here.

# What have you landed on in your stack journey?

Some questions I'd love your perspective on, if you've run into the same stuff:

1. **The orchestrator pattern for balance.** Am I overcomplicating this? Should I just be using one model for everything? 
2. **Animation tooling for stylized characters.** What's actually working for you at production quality in May 2026?
3. **Where you draw the AI-vs-human line on narrative.** I've drawn mine at canon vs. expansion. What's yours?
4. **Test infrastructure when AI writes most of your code.** I belatedly realized my bottleneck is QA, not code. Anyone built a setup they're happy with?
5. **One thing you wish you'd known at the start.** The big one. I've got my list above; I'd like to hear yours.

On my front, the game itself is in the public-building phase at [FantasyFantasy.io](http://FantasyFantasy.io) if you want to poke around (the current site has links to discussion/community/etc). I'm evolving this stack everyday, so if you've found something that could better solve some of the problems I've talked about, I'm all ears.
